summary: Presents a framework for recovery in MPLS networks. To deliver reliable service, label switching routers need procedures for fault detection, fault notification and fault recovery, and signaling must support configuring recovery. It describes the concepts and terminology for protecting traffic on different paths.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3469 describes ways to restore traffic after a failure in a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) network. It provides terms and comparison criteria rather than a complete recovery protocol.

subtitle: A framework for detecting MPLS faults and restoring traffic over recovery paths.

tldr.problem: IP routing may take several seconds or minutes to recover from a fault, while some services need restoration in seconds or tens of milliseconds.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes rerouting and protection switching, fault detection and notification, recovery timing, path scope and criteria for comparing recovery schemes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3469 is an Informational framework, not a protocol specification, and the supplied metadata says RFC 5462 updates it.

today: RFC 3469 is an Informational RFC published in February 2003 and has been updated by RFC 5462. It presents a conceptual framework rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: Why MPLS Recovery Is Needed
sections.content:
The RFC says interior gateway routing can take several seconds to recover from a fault, while Border Gateway Protocol can take minutes. Some services require restoration in seconds or tens of milliseconds, and IP routing may not provide equivalent bandwidth on an alternate path.

MPLS recovery can protect selected traffic and use paths configured for that purpose. The memo is conceptual: it describes motivation, goals and terminology, not a specific mechanism, policy or routing plan.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing can take longer to recover than some services can tolerate. The label-switching network can use a prepared recovery path or set up a new path after a fault.

sections.title: Rerouting and Protection Switching
sections.content:
Rerouting establishes a new path or path segment after a fault, using signaling. Protection switching prepares a recovery path before a fault and switches traffic to it when the fault is detected.

The two approaches can be combined. A system may switch traffic to a prepared recovery path quickly, then reroute later after routing has converged.
sections.plainLanguage: Rerouting builds a path after a failure. Protection switching prepares a path in advance and moves traffic to it when needed.

sections.title: Timing the Recovery Process
sections.content:
The MPLS recovery cycle divides recovery into five intervals: fault detection, hold-off, notification, recovery operation and traffic recovery. The hold-off interval is a configured wait that can allow lower-layer protection to act first; it may be zero.

The memo also describes reversion after a fault clears and dynamic rerouting after routing protocols converge. A Fault Indication Signal (FIS) notifies a Point of Repair; a Fault Recovery Signal (FRS) reports that a fault has been repaired.
sections.plainLanguage: The recovery cycle measures the time to detect a fault, notify the repair point and restore traffic. Separate cycles describe returning traffic to a preferred path or moving it to a newly selected path.

sections.title: Recovery Scope and Resource Choices
sections.content:
Recovery can apply to one link, a neighboring node, a longer path or a portion of traffic. A Path Switch LSR (PSL) moves or copies traffic between paths, while a Path Merge LSR (PML) receives recovery traffic and merges or delivers it.

In 1+1 protection, the recovery path carries a copy and the PML chooses between paths. In 1:1 protection, the recovery path may carry lower-priority traffic until the working path fails. Recovery paths may be pre-established or set up on demand, and their resources may be reserved in advance or when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A recovery plan can protect one link, a longer path or selected traffic. It can reserve capacity for recovery or let other traffic use that capacity until a failure occurs.

sections.title: Comparing Recovery Schemes
sections.content:
The memo proposes comparing schemes by recovery time, full restoration time, time spent unprotected, backup capacity, added latency, packet reordering, state overhead, packet loss and fault coverage.

It defines recovery time as the sum of detection, hold-off, notification, recovery operation and traffic restoration times. The Security Considerations section says the framework raises no security issues beyond those already present in MPLS; confidentiality on recovery paths is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Compare recovery plans by how quickly they restore traffic, how much capacity they need and which failures they cover. The memo does not define confidentiality for a recovery path.
